entry.title: CLIO in 2026: from agent to marketplace
entry.summary: In 2026, CLIO, the agent layer of IOWarp, grew from a runtime and a tool kit into a science agent, a desktop app, a coding agent and a marketplace of agents.
entry.content:
CLIO is the agent layer of IOWarp, GRC's platform for managing scientific data and context for AI. In February 2026 it had two parts, a storage runtime and a tool kit. By November 13 it had six, each with its own release schedule, and together they had published more than 300 tagged releases on GitHub this year. This is a tour of what each part does and how it got there.

The base: CLIO Core and CLIO Kit​

CLIO Core provides the storage and runtime services underneath everything else: it keeps data and context on distributed, tiered storage close to where agents and applications need it. Core shipped 24 releases between version 0.6.5 on February 23 and version 2.4.1 on November 11. Version 2.3.0, released October 9, brought the GPU runtime up on Intel GPUs, raising the number of passing tests on Argonne's Aurora system from 104 to 254. The same release served HDF5 reads from the CLIO cache tier, cut the latency of a cross-node collective operation by 3.1 times, and fixed seven crash-consistency bugs found across five fault scenarios. Luke Logan leads Core development.

CLIO Kit connects agents to scientific and HPC tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. It went from version 2.0.1 in February to 2.12.7 in November, about 60 releases in all. Jaime Cernuda and Isa Muradli are its main contributors.

An agent for science: CLIO Agent and its desktop​

CLIO Agent made its first 2026 release, version 0.3.1, on April 27, and reached version 0.9.7 on November 13 after nearly 90 releases. Version 0.9.0 in July added three ways to control what the agent does: a planning mode in which the agent may write only its plan until a person approves it, project hooks that run a lab's own scripts before or after each action, and sessions that loop, pursue a stated goal or run on a schedule. All three go through one permission system, where a deny rule always beats an allow.

Version 0.9.7 builds web and scholarly search into the agent. Its literature tools query OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv, Europe PMC, OSTI.gov, DataCite and OpenCitations, and ask before the first query to each source. Deep research now delivers its report with full references, and the agent can see the plots and page renders its own scripts open. Long conversions and builds run until they finish instead of hitting a fixed time limit.

People reach the agent through GACT TUI, a terminal and desktop front end that can drive any compliant agent back end. It went from version 0.2.1 in April to 0.13.0 on November 13, about 60 releases. Version 0.13 adds Spanish, Japanese and Greek to the interface, marked as machine translations until native speakers review them, along with a guided tour for new users. Cernuda leads the agent and its front end.

A marketplace of science agents​

The CLIO Agent Marketplace holds the agents and shared capabilities that CLIO Agent loads. Its first release, version 0.5.2 on June 17, shipped agents that analyze EarthScope GNSS station data through the National Data Platform; they passed all seven tasks of the team's test matrix with three different open-weight models.

Version 0.7.0, released October 28, replaced that first layout with agent classes and capability plugins that agents can combine. It introduced CLIO Data, which inspects, checks and converts HDF5, netCDF-4, ADIOS2 and Parquet data and keeps its conversion checks with its procedures. Its deep-research guidance records verified claims, rejected claims and open gaps separately, so a report shows which evidence still needs checking. Version 0.8.0 followed on November 13, the twelfth marketplace release of the year.

CLIO Coder​

CLIO Coder is an open-source coding agent for scientific software and everyday engineering. The experimental first release on April 24 already ran worker processes for batch tasks, kept a record of every run and gated tool access through three safety modes. About 60 releases later, version 0.8.0 on November 13 targets people who run a coding agent beside colleagues, other agents and scripts, such as researchers on a shared login node. Two sessions can share a folder safely, the sandbox hides credentials and token files from contained commands, and headless runs end with one machine-readable result for automation. A per-project store keeps results and datasets outside the working tree, and diagnostic reports are shown to the user before anything leaves the machine. A new guide covers installing it on HPC login nodes. Anthony Kougkas leads its development.

Around the stack​

Two releases outside the CLIO repositories support the same work. Jarvis-CD 1.8, released August 6 and maintained by Logan, ships execution profiles for scientific applications, services and I/O interceptors that the maintainers keep current, the same ones used in a cross-cluster evaluation campaign. It also reconciles Slurm jobs that never reached the Jarvis runtime against live and accounting state.

FITS-HDF5-VOL, released May 6 and written by Muradli, lets HDF5 programs read FITS astronomy files without converting them. It is a read-only HDF5 Virtual Object Layer connector, so tools such as h5py and h5dump open an unmodified FITS file and read its pixels, tables and headers. It is validated against HDF5 1.14.x and 2.1.x with 162 tests, including the astropy test corpus and files from NRAO.

CLIO will be shown at the HDF5 birds-of-a-feather session at SC26 on November 19; see GRC at SC26.

entry.title: GRC at SC26: a visitor's guide
entry.summary: SC26 runs November 15 to 20 in Chicago. Here is where to find GRC's six workshop talks, four posters, one paper, the SPOTTER-AI demo and the HDF5 BoF.
entry.content:
SC26, the International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis, runs November 15 to 20 at McCormick Place in Chicago, less than two miles from the Illinois Tech campus. GRC brings six workshop talks, four research posters and one paper, plus a live SPOTTER-AI demo at the DOE booth and an HDF5 birds-of-a-feather session with a CLIO demo. This guide lists every session by day, with times in Chicago time (CST).

Monday, November 16: workshops​

Two talks come from work with Hariharan Devarajan, a GRC alumnus now at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, at the ProTools workshop in room W176c:

  • 10:30 to 10:54 a.m. Orion, an observability framework for I/O monitoring in hybrid, workflow-centric HPC systems, with Izzet Yildirim.
  • 10:54 to 11:18 a.m. DataCrumbs, which captures data across the layers of an HPC storage stack to explain I/O performance, with Neeraj Rajesh.

Four more are at the PDSW workshop in room W179b:

  • 10:50 to 11:10 a.m. GPUH5, by Joshua Fernandes, lets a GPU kernel write HDF5-style data without leaving the kernel. On a Gray-Scott simulation writing 380 snapshots, it hides 96% of the I/O and finishes 1.9 times faster than default HDF5.
  • 11:30 to 11:50 a.m. GDSight, by Yildirim, traces each NVMe command issued through GPUDirect Storage back to the application operation that caused it.
  • 12:15 to 12:20 p.m. A work-in-progress talk on trigger-gated multimodal LLM agents that monitor simulations in situ, by Hua Xu.
  • 4:45 to 4:50 p.m. A work-in-progress talk on type-safe, dynamically defined metadata, led by Josh Teves of Sandia National Laboratories with GRC and Oak Ridge coauthors.

Tuesday, November 17: posters​

All four research posters are on display from 10:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. in the Skyline Ballroom North Pre-Function area:

  • ToolFuse (Yildirim) merges identical tool calls that many LLM agents issue at once. In its test, 16 equivalent requests became one execution and used 11.79 times less CPU time.
  • StageOnce (Yildirim) stages each input once for a whole fleet of agent jobs on a node, cutting fleet run time by 31% to 51% at 12 concurrent jobs.
  • Extending I/O observability to explainability (Rajesh) goes from measuring I/O to explaining it, so optimizations can target the cause.
  • GNNs beyond HBM (Rajni Pawar) streams compressed, bit-exact features so graph neural networks can train on more data than GPU memory holds.

Wednesday, November 18: a demo and a paper​

12:00 to 1:00 p.m., DOE booth 4829, station 2. Bogdan Nicolae and Jaime Cernuda demonstrate SPOTTER-AI, which detects tampered data in scientific AI workflows and traces it back to its source. The demo repeats through the hour. SPOTTER-AI is one of GRC's two Genesis Mission projects.

4:30 to 5:00 p.m., room W181abc. Trigger, Render, Reason, by Xu, is GRC's paper in the technical program. Simulations can run to completion while computing the wrong answer, a waste the paper calls dark waste. Its system, Vigil, adds lightweight science-aware checks to a running simulation; when one fires, the flagged data is rendered as images and a multimodal model judges whether the science is still valid, so the run can be stopped or restarted from a checkpoint. Across four simulation codes, Vigil caught every deliberately configured failure with no false alarms. It builds on the in situ operators Xu presented at eScience 2026.

The paper appears in "Papers in Conversation: Scientific AI at Extreme Scale", a session that closes with a panel of its authors and is livestreamed, so it can be followed from outside Chicago.

Thursday, November 19: HDF5 birds of a feather​

12:15 to 1:15 p.m., room W185d. Anthony Kougkas joins speakers from The HDF Group, LifeBoat, Ohio State University and NVIDIA for "Trustworthy Data at Scale: HDF5 in the Age of AI-Driven Science". The session includes a demo of CLIO, IOWarp's agent stack, which grew into a family of releases this year.

Meet the team​

Kougkas also serves on the SC26 State of the Practice committee. Xian-He Sun is a coauthor on most of the work above. The GRC at SC26 page has the full schedule with calendar files, links to each session in the SC26 program, and whom to contact about collaboration, CLIO and the SPOTTER-AI demo.

entry.title: ChronoLog's year: from 2.5 to 3.5
entry.summary: Eleven ChronoLog releases between April and November 2026 added SQL and publish-subscribe access, made writes durable and moved to a new HPC software stack.
entry.content:
Between April 2 and November 12, the ChronoLog team published eleven releases, from 2.5.0 to 3.5.0. Over those seven months, GRC's distributed log store gained SQL, publish-subscribe and agent interfaces. It also learned to keep every event it acknowledges, even through a crash, and moved to a current HPC software stack. This is a summary of the year, release by release.

ChronoLog is a distributed shared log that orders events by physical time and moves them from memory to local storage to an HDF5 archive. ChronoKeepers take in events, ChronoGraphers merge them into story chunks and write the archive, and ChronoPlayers serve replays. The project is funded by an NSF CSSI framework grant (OAC-2104013) led by Xian-He Sun.

Spring: packaging and new read paths (2.5 to 2.8)​

  • 2.5.0 (April 2) added range, earliest and latest reads to ChronoKVS, the key-value interface, along with a native Grafana data source plugin and a first streaming plugin. It also set up a release pipeline with Docker images and launched a new website and documentation at chronolog.dev.
  • 2.6.0 (April 24) split the configuration, shipped source tarballs and RPM and Debian packages, and added end-to-end data-integrity tests.
  • 2.7.0 (April 30) separated the client library from the server's internal data structures and added a protocol version check when a client connects.
  • 2.8.0 (May 18) added extraction chains, which control where sealed chunks go next, and a configurable number of ingestion threads.

3.0 and 3.1: new ways in​

ChronoLog 3.0.0 (May 29) added ChronoSQL, which queries stories with SQL-style statements, and ChronoPubSub, a publish-subscribe plugin. It moved the ChronoLog MCP server, which gives AI agents access to the log, into the main repository. The release also added a recording service to ChronoPlayer and cleaned up the client API.

Version 3.1.0 (September 7) merged replay streams in ChronoPlayer, let clients read the last N events of a story straight from keeper memory, and added a store plugin for the Lightweight Distributed Metric Service (LDMS), a monitoring service for HPC systems. Version 3.1.1 followed on September 10.

Autumn: never lose an event (3.2 to 3.4)​

The fall releases closed the gaps in which an event could be lost.

  • 3.2.0 (October 2) keeps each sealed chunk on its keeper until the grapher confirms that the archive holds it. Until then, a chunk the grapher had received but not yet written existed only in the grapher's memory. Replays now read events that are not archived yet directly from the keepers, and an incomplete answer is reported as partial instead of looking complete.
  • 3.3.0 (October 15) has each grapher record every archive file it publishes in a manifest, and players find files only through those records. On NFS, a directory listing can be stale, so a replay could miss a file written late. Each story also gets its own directory.
  • 3.4.0 (November 5) adds opt-in durable writes. A durable write returns success only after the keeper has written the event to a write-ahead log on local disk and synced it, and a restarted keeper replays its log into the archive. With eight writers, a 1 KB durable write took about 480 microseconds at the median on a local NVMe drive, about 15,000 events per second. The unit test suite grew from 480 to 758 tests.

3.5: a new dependency stack​

ChronoLog had built with Spack 0.21.2 since 2024. Version 3.5.0 (November 12) moves to Spack 1.2.2, with Mercury 2.4.1, Margo 0.24.4, Thallium 0.17.0, libfabric 2.6.0 and HDF5 2.2.0. The newer Margo stops a memory leak and supports deadlines that the next release will use for RPCs that still wait without one. Because the newer Mercury handles requests differently, 3.5.0 cannot talk to 3.4.0 or older, and every component and client has to be upgraded together. Archives written by 3.4.0 remain readable.

The people behind the releases​

Research software engineer Eneko Gonzalez led the work from 2.5 through 3.0, including the release pipeline, ChronoKVS, ChronoSQL, ChronoPubSub and the MCP server. Research software engineer Kun Feng wrote the Grafana and LDMS plugins and led 3.1 through 3.5, including durable retention, the manifest archive, the write-ahead log and the new stack. Research associate Inna Brodkin rebuilt the configuration manager and wrote the extraction chains, the player's recording service and its combined replay stream. Shivalika Chaudhary, a 2025 summer resident, wrote the first streaming plugin.

Jaime Cernuda and Anthony Kougkas presented a ChronoLog poster at the NSF CSSI principal investigators' meeting in Rockville, Maryland, from September 13 to 15. In May, a GCASR 2026 poster showed ChronoLog feeding live HPC telemetry to Grafana and serving AI agents through MCP.

entry.title: Autumn papers at eScience and PACT 2026
entry.summary: Four GRC papers at IEEE eScience 2026 add systems support for science agents and in situ analysis; at PACT 2026, a paper speeds block-sparse transformers.
entry.content:
AI agents are starting to do scientific work: finding data, running tools and producing results. That raises systems questions. Does a workflow of agents recover when one of them makes a mistake? How does an agent find the right file? Can storage use the time an agent spends thinking? GRC students answered all three in papers at IEEE eScience 2026, along with a fourth on in situ analysis, and a fifth paper at PACT 2026 addressed transformers on GPUs.

The 22nd IEEE International Conference on eScience took place in Naples, Italy, from September 28 to October 2, and all four GRC papers appeared in its main track. PACT 2026, the International Conference on Parallel Architectures and Compilation Techniques, ran from October 19 to 22 at the Discovery Partners Institute in Chicago.

Testing how agent workflows recover from errors​

Workflows built from several large language model (LLM) agents now run multi-step computational tasks, but little is known about how they cope with bad inputs, failed tools or small numerical errors. In Agent Error Simulator, Keith Bateman presents a benchmark framework that injects faults on purpose. It sits as a transparent proxy between the agents and the model and injects format, logic and tool-call faults at chosen points in a planner, worker and aggregator workflow.

The team ran 194 jobs in 10 test groups on four open models from 2 billion to 32 billion parameters. Format and tool-call faults were recovered by every model. Logic faults were not: the 27 and 32 billion parameter models recovered from a wrong value injected into an earlier step, while the 7 and 2 billion parameter models carried it forward. A logic error injected into the aggregator, the agent that combines the others' results, caused every model to fail. The benchmark suite, injection tools and result data are released for others to reuse. The work is part of the DTIO project, with Jaime Cernuda, Luke Logan, Bogdan Nicolae and Franck Cappello of Argonne, Xian-He Sun and Anthony Kougkas.

Search that agents do not have to guess​

LLM agents usually look for files with guesses: glob patterns, grep and file reads, repeated until something matches. This costs tool calls and tokens and ignores the metadata inside scientific file formats. Acropolis, by Rajni Pawar, adds content indexing to a tiered file system, summarizing each file as it is written, and offers search to agents through an MCP server, with lexical, vector and graph search engines behind one interface.

On a 70-query benchmark over CMIP6 climate data, an agent using Acropolis found files as accurately as one using shell tools, with about one third fewer tool calls per query and about 3.1 times fewer LLM tokens. The work builds on IOWarp and LABIOS.

Staging data while the agent thinks​

Agents working on scientific data spend most of their time inside tool calls that read from storage. Before each call, a reasoning model thinks, and storage sits idle while the files the next tool needs start to appear in that reasoning. AgentStage, by Izzet Yildirim, reads the agent's streaming reasoning and its file system probes to infer which files come next. It copies them to fast local storage, decompressing on the way, so the tool's reads are served from fast storage.

Across four reasoning models, AgentStage made curated scientific tasks 1.74 times faster on average and up to 2.34 times faster in a single run, and sped up tasks from the MLE-bench, KramaBench and DSBench benchmarks by up to 1.36 times. The paper also shows how to estimate in advance whether a task will benefit, since compute-bound tasks or tasks that touch many files gain less.

Derived quantities inside the I/O path​

Simulations produce more data than can be written as often as scientists would like, so analysis has to happen in situ, while the data is produced. Hua Xu's paper, Rich I/O-centric Derived Quantity Operators, adds pluggable operators to the ADIOS2 I/O library that compute derived quantities as data is written. Some operators need only the current timestep, such as one that finds vortex cores. Others need earlier timesteps or earlier runs, such as a temporal derivative or a checksum that confirms a rerun matches the original. A metadata layer runs the operators at each step and records every result, with CLIO Core from IOWarp as the I/O manager that keeps history on tiered storage. Each operator declares what it will need, and that drives which data is kept on the fastest tier.

The team tested the framework on three platforms, including the Frontier supercomputer at Oak Ridge, and released the code as part of Coeus. Xu wrote the paper with Cernuda, Kougkas and Sun and with collaborators from Oak Ridge, Argonne, Los Alamos and Sandia national laboratories, the University of Tennessee and Rochester Institute of Technology.

Block-sparse transformers on GPUs​

At PACT 2026, Lihan Hu presented "Improving Data Reuse across Blocks for Efficient Block-Sparse Transformers on GPUs" on October 22, in the session on performance optimization, scheduling and communication. The paper, with Xiaoyang Lu, Sun and Peng Jiang, reuses data across the blocks of block-sparse transformer models to make them run more efficiently on GPUs.

entry.title: GRC joins DOE's Genesis Mission with Argonne and PNNL
entry.summary: DOE selected SPOTTER-AI, led by Argonne, and Portus, led by PNNL, among the first Genesis Mission projects. GRC is a co-PI on both and contributes CLIO.
entry.content:
GRC is a partner in two of the first projects of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. SPOTTER-AI, led by Argonne National Laboratory, protects AI-driven science workflows from tampered data. Portus, led by Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL), helps coding agents run scientific workflows well on HPC and cloud systems. GRC is a co-principal investigator on both and brings CLIO, the agent layer of IOWarp.

The Genesis Mission​

Through the Genesis Mission, DOE is building the American Science Cloud, a national platform where researchers share datasets, models and workflows and use AI to speed up discovery. On July 22, DOE posted the list of the first projects selected for award negotiations under the mission. Both projects with GRC are on it, and work on both began on August 1.

SPOTTER-AI: guarding AI workflows from tampered data​

Openness is what makes a shared science platform useful, and it is also a risk. A few tampered images or one corrupted data source can quietly skew an AI model and spread through many downstream studies, with no record of where the error entered. Conventional cybersecurity protects the infrastructure, so these attacks on the data itself slip through.

SPOTTER-AI, short for Scientific Provenance-Oriented Threat Tracing and Attribution for Genesis Workflows, works in three steps:

  • Track. It records each workflow's full history, every dataset, model step and tool call, as provenance.
  • Detect. It asks whether a piece of data should have mattered as much as it did to a result. A transformer model combines provenance with signals such as attention scores to tell legitimate high-impact inputs from tampered ones.
  • Trace. When something looks wrong, an AI agent reasons backward through the workflow's history to find the source of the attack and describe how it happened.

Because it inspects only the suspicious parts of a workflow, SPOTTER-AI's advantage grows as workflows get larger. The team will first test it on a digital twin from one of the OPAL research projects, which predicts plant traits from images, sensor readings and genetics. Each piece is being built as a reusable American Science Cloud service.

Bogdan Nicolae of Argonne leads the project. The partners include Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Illinois Tech. At GRC, Anthony Kougkas and Xian-He Sun lead the work with Jaime Cernuda, contributing CLIO Core, CLIO Kit, CLIO Agent and CLIO Coder.

Portus: performance portability for agentic workflows​

Agentic workflows change their execution paths as they run, generate new pieces on the fly, and must cope with computing resources that contend, fail and change. Without better orchestration, scientists would have to tune every port to a new system by hand or accept large performance losses.

Portus starts from the observation that agentic workflows are built from a small vocabulary of recurring patterns. It breaks workflows into producer-consumer building blocks and learns models of how they perform that carry over from one workflow to another. A coding agent can then use those models to find bottlenecks in newly generated workflow code, rank alternatives and map it to the resources available. The models keep learning from live telemetry, because a fixed training set cannot keep up with changing workflows and resources.

Nathan Tallent of PNNL leads the project. GRC's part covers performance models for producer-consumer data flow and a storage model for data placement, while CLIO provides context and data services to the agents. Kougkas and Sun lead the GRC work with Xiaoyang Lu and Luke Logan.

Two partnerships, one software stack​

Both projects build on long collaborations. With Nicolae, GRC works on I/O for scientific AI, including PKAS at HPDC 2026. With Tallent's group at PNNL, GRC worked on DaYu and DataFlowDrs, tools that analyze how data flows through workflows. DataFlowDrs was accepted by IEEE TPDS this summer. In both projects, CLIO gives AI agents access to scientific data, tools and context on HPC systems.

Update (November 2026): Nicolae and Cernuda demonstrate SPOTTER-AI at the DOE booth (4829, station 2) at SC26 in Chicago on Wednesday, November 18, from 12:00 to 1:00 p.m. See GRC at SC26.

entry.title: Three new PhD students join GRC
entry.summary: Ainara Garcia and Anwar Benhnini start with the fall 2026 term on MPI4AI and UniMCC, joining Zia Uddin Chowdhury, who began in January on IOWarp.
entry.content:
Ainara Garcia and Anwar Benhnini began their PhDs in the Department of Computer Science at Illinois Institute of Technology with the fall 2026 term, which started on August 17, and joined the Gnosis Research Center. They complete a 2026 cohort with Zia Uddin Chowdhury, who arrived in January and has already presented his first GRC poster.

Ainara Garcia: communication for AI at scale​

Garcia earned a BS in Computer Engineering from Clemson University. She is advised by Xian-He Sun and Bogdan Nicolae and works on MPI4AI, an NSF Frameworks project led at Illinois Tech by Nicolae with Tennessee Technological University, the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and Stony Brook University. MPI4AI extends Open MPI, the open-source implementation of the Message Passing Interface, with native GPU communication, collective operations designed for AI, integration with compute streams and fault tolerance. The project targets three AI patterns: neural architecture search with transfer learning, key-value prefix caching in LLM inference, and large-scale data-parallel training. It also aims to carry its extensions into the MPI-5 and MPI-6 standards.

Anwar Benhnini: memory-centric computing​

Benhnini is advised by Xiaoyang Lu and Sun and works on UniMCC, an NSF Computer Systems Research project shared with the University of Iowa. UniMCC is building a full-stack system for hardware that pairs near-memory data processors with a disaggregated, shared memory pool. The work crosses layers: architecture, hardware and software interfaces, compiler support, runtimes and performance models. Sun is the principal investigator of the Illinois Tech award and Lu leads the project in the lab. In 2026 Lu was first author on two UniMCC papers about long-sequence LLM inference: an I/O analysis of attention at ASPLOS and a processing-in-memory accelerator for hybrid sparse attention at IPDPS.

Zia Uddin Chowdhury: KV cache survivability​

Chowdhury joined in January 2026, advised by Anthony Kougkas and Sun, and works on IOWarp. At the 13th Greater Chicago Area Systems Research Workshop (GCASR 2026) at Northwestern University on May 11, he presented the poster "Pre-RoPE versus Post-RoPE: Trading Per-Step Compute for KVCache Survivability", with Jaime Cernuda, Jie Ye, Kougkas and Sun.

LLM inference engines cache attention keys and values so they are not recomputed at every decoding step. The usual approach stores keys after applying rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which bakes each token's position into the cache. When a long context overflows and the oldest tokens are dropped, the surviving keys carry stale positions. Storing keys before RoPE and rotating them at attention time avoids that problem but costs compute on every step.

The poster measured both sides of the trade-off with vLLM and Llama 3.1 8B Instruct on NVIDIA GH200 nodes of the Delta system, using LongBench NarrativeQA at 4K to 32K context lengths. Pre-RoPE storage raised time to first token by 10% to 30% and lowered decode throughput by 1.8 to 3.1 times. In return, when half of the cache was truncated, re-rotating pre-RoPE keys took about 30 times less time than the re-prefill baseline, while naive slicing of a post-RoPE cache inflated perplexity by 30 to 65 times.

entry.title: PKAS and Metis at HPDC 2026
entry.summary: At HPDC 2026 in Cleveland, PKAS schedules LLM inference by predicting KV cache use, and Metis uses LLM agents to explain the I/O behavior of HPC software.
entry.content:
Two papers with GRC authors appeared at the 35th International Symposium on High-Performance Parallel and Distributed Computing (HPDC 2026), held in Cleveland from July 13 to 16. PKAS, which Jie Ye presented on July 14, schedules LLM inference by predicting how much KV cache memory each request will need. Metis, in the REX-IO workshop, uses LLM agents to explain what HPC I/O functions do.

PKAS: admitting requests with the future in mind​

LLM inference engines keep a KV cache of attention states so they do not recompute them for every new token. The cache grows with sequence length and batch size and easily outgrows GPU memory. To keep GPUs busy, engines such as vLLM use continuous batching: they mix new requests, which process a prompt (prefill), with ongoing requests that generate tokens (decode).

The schedulers that decide which new requests to admit look only at the memory free for the next step. They do not account for the KV cache those requests will need as they decode. When the cache overflows, the engine preempts requests and later recomputes them, which hurts both throughput and latency.

PKAS, short for Predictive KV Cache-Aware Scheduling, runs a low-overhead simulation of future KV cache use and combines it with a lightweight prediction of output length to decide whether a candidate request can be admitted safely. The team built PKAS into vLLM's scheduling interface and compared it with vLLM's default first-come, first-served scheduler and with a learning-to-rank scheduler. The tests ran on Argonne's Polaris system, with Llama 3.1 8B and a mixture-of-experts coding model, on two long-context datasets (NarrativeQA and codeU, with average inputs of 24,000 and 31,500 tokens) and on ShareGPT conversations. PKAS reached up to 7.34 times higher throughput and 8 times lower latency, with the largest gains on long-context workloads where KV cache pressure is highest.

The authors are Ye, Avinash Maurya and Bogdan Nicolae of Argonne National Laboratory, Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata of Red Hat, Anthony Kougkas and Xian-He Sun. The work is part of DeepIO, GRC's research on I/O for scientific AI.

Metis: agents that explain I/O behavior​

Explaining why an HPC application's I/O is slow requires knowing what each I/O function means and what role it plays at runtime, across every layer of the software stack. Experts still do much of this characterization by hand, which does not scale and is hard to reproduce as I/O libraries grow more complex.

Metis uses agentic LLMs to combine different sources of evidence about each function, and measures how far the agents agree. Compared with a baseline built on Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, Metis generalized better to function categories it had not seen (0.90 versus 0.35), finished in 27.7 seconds instead of 84.5, and characterized 41.8 functions per minute instead of 14.28. Under federated scaling, its verifier sustained 330,000 to 1.18 million functions per second. The authors applied it to the behavior of the HDF5 library.

Neeraj Rajesh of GRC wrote Metis with Karim Youssef and Hariharan Devarajan of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Sarah Neuwirth of Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz.

Update (July 2026): On July 29 the lab released WisIO 0.2.0, its open-source tool that connects I/O bottlenecks in workflow traces to their root causes. Every Python version that 0.1.1 supported had reached end of life, so the release moves to Python 3.10 through 3.13. Small analysis views now run in pandas instead of Dask, which cut one DFTracer analysis from 68 to 19 seconds. Each reported bottleneck now states why it is severe, and a new web app lets users upload a trace and read the findings.

entry.title: Two journal articles on recoverable memory and workflow data flow
entry.summary: ACM TOS publishes NVREC, a recommendation system that recovers from failure in non-volatile memory, and IEEE TPDS accepts DataFlowDrs for HPC workflows.
entry.content:
Two long-running lines of GRC research reached journals this summer. On July 8, ACM Transactions on Storage published NVREC, a recommendation system that trains in non-volatile memory and can recover after a failure. IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems accepted DataFlowDrs, a suite of tools from Pacific Northwest National Laboratory (PNNL) and GRC that finds and fixes data flow bottlenecks in HPC workflows. It will appear in the December issue.

NVREC: checkpoints that live in memory​

Recommendation models hold very large embedding tables. Current training systems assume memory is volatile, so they periodically checkpoint model weights and embeddings to slower solid-state drives in case of failure. That design cannot take advantage of non-volatile memory (NVM), which keeps its contents when power is lost.

NVREC trains on a hybrid of DRAM and NVM and checkpoints in memory. It uses three techniques:

  • It splits the embeddings so that only popular vectors sit in DRAM, which hides the higher latency of NVM.
  • It keeps two versions of each vector in NVM, one persistent copy for crash recovery and one runtime copy for training updates, and alternates between them.
  • It uses fine-grained parallelism to hide the cost of checkpointing the model parameters held in DRAM and on the GPU.

On synthetic and real-world datasets, NVREC trained 1.05 to 6.85 times faster than existing systems and checkpointed more than 5 times faster.

The authors are Ping Chen, Shuibing He, Peiyi Hong, Siling Yang, Tong Wu and Gang Chen of Zhejiang University, Xuechen Zhang of Kennesaw State University, and Xian-He Sun. He, now a professor at Zhejiang University, is a former postdoctoral researcher in Sun's group.

DataFlowDrs: diagnosing data flow in HPC workflows​

Scientific workflows on HPC systems move large amounts of data between tasks, and the bottlenecks often appear in storage and I/O networks. Earlier work covered workflow coordination, scheduling and storage systems, but no tool suite could automatically find where data flow was holding a workflow back.

DataFlowDrs fills that gap with five parts:

  • lightweight, high-resolution measurement and visualization of workflow data flow
  • fast modeling that compresses repeated coordination patterns to shrink the analysis data
  • interpretable models, generated automatically, that predict how data flow scales
  • analysis that quantifies and ranks bottlenecks for different mixes of task parallelism and storage
  • new schedules and resource assignments that resolve the bottlenecks

On a representative set of workflows, DataFlowDrs improved performance over baseline and earlier methods by choosing the right trade-off between task parallelism and storage performance. Student teams reproduced the work in the Student Cluster Competition at SC24, and the article summarizes their findings. The suite is open source and includes DaYu, the HDF5 data flow analysis tool that Meng Tang of GRC first-authored at IEEE Cluster 2024.

The authors are Nathan Tallent, Jesun Firoz, Zhen Peng and Luanzheng Guo of PNNL, together with Tang, Anthony Kougkas and Sun of GRC.

entry.title: Spring 2026 papers: LLM inference meets the memory hierarchy
entry.summary: Papers at ASPLOS, EACL, DATE and IPDPS 2026 attack data movement in long-context LLM inference, from hardware prefetching up to KV cache pruning.
entry.content:
Between March and May 2026, GRC researchers and their collaborators presented four papers on one problem: long-context LLM inference is limited by how data moves through the memory hierarchy, not only by compute. The papers appeared at ASPLOS, EACL, DATE and IPDPS, and their answers range from a hardware prefetcher to KV cache pruning. A fifth paper, also at IPDPS, applies the same I/O lens to HPC workflows.

The I/O cost of attention (ASPLOS)​

Self-attention, the core of transformer models, needs memory that grows with the square of the sequence length. At ASPLOS 2026 in Pittsburgh (March 22 to 26), Xiaoyang Lu and Xian-He Sun, with Boyu Long, Xiaoming Chen and Yinhe Han of the Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, asked how far careful I/O analysis can take an accelerator for it.

The paper first derives an I/O analysis for tall-and-skinny matrix multiplication, which captures the dominant data movement of long-sequence attention. From that analysis the authors build AttenIO, an accelerator for exact long-sequence self-attention with three optimizations: analytically derived tiling and scheduling that minimize I/O, three-level overlap of communication and computation to hide I/O stalls, and parallel execution patterns for softmax. AttenIO runs 1.6 to 8.8 times faster than the best existing solutions the authors compared against. The authors argue that the method reaches beyond attention, as a principled way to guide I/O optimization in general.

Processing in memory for sparse attention (IPDPS)​

LLM inference has two stages with different bottlenecks. The prefill stage, which processes the prompt, carries the quadratic cost of attention; the decoding stage, which produces one token at a time, is bound by memory. Sparse attention cuts the cost of prefill, but moving data between processor and memory still limits the GPU.

At IPDPS 2026 in New Orleans (May 25 to 29), Lu and Sun, with Lihan Hu and Peng Jiang of the University of Iowa, GRC's partner on UniMCC, and Hongrui Huang of Columbia University, presented PILOT. It places processing units inside memory to run hybrid sparse attention during prefill and both dense and sparse attention during decoding, and uses I/O analysis to choose tiling and scheduling inside the processing-in-memory hardware. Paired with a GPU, PILOT runs sparse prefill attention up to 19.96 times faster and decoding attention up to 57.11 times faster than the GPU baseline, and speeds up end-to-end long-sequence inference by up to 5.31 times compared with a conventional GPU system.

A prefetcher for memory-intensive workloads (DATE)​

There is growing interest in running LLMs locally on CPUs, for privacy and low latency. Attention on a CPU moves large amounts of data between the cache hierarchy and DRAM, which is where hardware prefetchers help, but current prefetchers struggle with diverse and changing access patterns.

At DATE 2026 in Verona (April 20 to 22), Vadim Biryukov, Lu and Sun, with Zirui Liu of the University of Minnesota and Kaixiong Zhou of North Carolina State University, presented Zion. It combines independent temporal and spatial modules to cover a broad range of access patterns, and uses runtime feedback to keep prefetching efficient under memory pressure. In multi-core evaluations, Zion improved performance by up to 43.2% on SPEC benchmarks and 43.0% on self-attention workloads compared with the best existing prefetchers.

Pruning the KV cache one page at a time (EACL Findings)​

The KV cache stores attention keys and values for earlier tokens so they are not recomputed, but it grows with every token. vLLM's PagedAttention keeps the cache in fixed-size blocks, and eviction methods that rank tokens by attention score do not fit, because the optimized attention kernels never return those scores.

PagedEviction, in the Findings of EACL 2026 (Rabat, March 24 to 29), ranks tokens using the key and value tensors instead. It evicts individual tokens during prefill and, during decoding, removes a whole block only after the newest block fills, so it needs no changes to the CUDA attention kernels. With Llama 3.2 1B and a 1,024-token cache budget, it reached up to 3,020 tokens per second, 37% more than keeping the full cache, and it cut latency by about 10% to 12% across 1B, 3B and 8B models. Jie Ye and Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata of Argonne share first authorship, with Siddhisanket Raskar of PNNL, Sun, Anthony Kougkas, Murali Emani, Venkatram Vishwanath and Bogdan Nicolae.

The same lens on HPC workflows (IPDPS)​

The second GRC paper at IPDPS turns I/O analysis to scientific workflows. Meng Tang, Kougkas and Sun, with Luanzheng Guo and Nathan Tallent of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, argue that I/O-aware schedulers look at tasks one at a time and miss workflow-level behavior such as file reuse and producer-consumer data exchange. Their workflow-centric method correlates workflow structure with I/O metrics across six HPC workflows, covering 3,500 task instances, 1,387 unique files and 1.5 TB of I/O. The patterns they found point to better task placement, data movement and storage selection.

entry.title: Twelve posters at GCASR 2026
entry.summary: At the 13th Greater Chicago Area Systems Research Workshop, GRC posters covered agent I/O, data discovery, provenance, logging, workflows and memory.
entry.content:
GRC researchers and collaborators presented twelve posters at the 13th Greater Chicago Area Systems Research Workshop (GCASR 2026) on May 11 at Northwestern University in Evanston. Taken together, the posters give a snapshot of the lab's work in spring 2026: how AI agents read and find scientific data, how multi-agent workflows run and recover, how workflows and logs move data, and how inference uses memory.

How agents read and find scientific data​

Correct is not I/O efficient. Izzet Yildirim, with Jie Ye, Jaime Cernuda, Xian-He Sun and Anthony Kougkas, traced the file operations of scientific workflows written by LLM coding agents. Of 105 agent-generated workflows across five tasks, 46 passed validation. Even the correct ones issued a median of 3.8 times more POSIX operations and read 6.5 times more data than expert implementations. The conclusion: storage behavior has to be measured directly before agent-written code runs on shared HPC or cloud storage.

Agentic search. Shazzadul Islam, with Cernuda, Sun and Kougkas, presented CLIO Search, a retrieval engine that profiles each data collection and then runs lexical, vector, graph and scientific-unit searches in parallel. The same LLM answered ten discovery queries over 341 National Data Platform datasets three ways. All three answered every query correctly, but the CLIO-backed agent used 52% fewer tokens and 91% less wall time than an agent relying on general web tools.

Semantic search for agent discovery. Rajni Pawar, with Luke Logan, Sun and Kougkas, embedded search inside the storage layer: file metadata is extracted, summarized by an LLM and indexed when data is written. On 273 astrophysics simulation files and 20 natural-language queries, a vector backend found the right file first 95% of the time, while BM25 keyword search inside the storage system answered in 0.047 milliseconds, 350 times faster than the same algorithm running as an external service.

Running and recovering multi-agent workflows​

Speculative dispatching. Ye, with Islam, Cernuda, Sun and Kougkas, applied speculative execution to the decision of which agent runs next. Agents start ahead of time while the full plan is computed; a reconciliation step keeps correct work, salvages partial matches and discards mispredictions. In preliminary results, the speculative planner produced dispatch plans with 0.50 to 0.78 similarity to the optimal plan at 4 to 10 times lower latency.

AgentRecall. Keith Bateman, with Sun and Kougkas, presented a provenance and rewind system for multi-agent workflows. It records tool calls, messages and prompts, stores them in IOWarp's hierarchical storage, and lets a person or an agent roll back to an earlier context when a mistake surfaces. Preliminary results showed rollback improving accuracy by up to 84% over baselines, with tool-call errors easier to fix than logical or formatting errors.

Trigger, Render, Reason. Hua Xu presented work on multimodal LLM agents that monitor scientific simulations with awareness of the science being simulated.

Workflows, logs and streams​

Storage mismatches. Meng Tang, with Luanzheng Guo and Nathan Tallent of PNNL, Kougkas and Sun, studied genomics and climate-tracking workflows on a production HPC cluster. I/O took 42% to 98% of total execution time, and choosing the fastest storage for each task on its own could make the whole workflow up to 6.8 times slower than a storage-aware choice, because of the data movement it forced between dependent tasks.

ChronoLog. Eneko Gonzalez, Kun Feng, Inna Brodkin, Kyle Chard of the University of Chicago, Kougkas and Sun presented ChronoLog, the lab's distributed log store that orders events by physical time, appends without locks, tiers data automatically and serves range queries. The poster showed two uses: live HPC telemetry in Grafana, and an MCP server that gives LLM agents a durable, replayable memory of past sessions.

StreamGuard. Hai Duc Nguyen, Bogdan Nicolae, Tekin Bicer, Amal Gueroudji, Matthieu Dorier, Chard and Ian Foster, of Argonne National Laboratory and the University of Chicago, presented low-overhead resilience for real-time HPC data streams.

Where files go. Neeraj Rajesh, with Sun and Kougkas, presented "Applications do I/O. What if files actually went... somewhere else?"

Inference and memory​

Pre-RoPE versus post-RoPE. Zia Uddin Chowdhury, with Cernuda, Ye, Kougkas and Sun, measured the trade-off between storing KV cache keys before or after rotary position embeddings. Storing them before costs compute at every decoding step but lets the cache survive truncation without re-running the prompt.

HyPIM. Jinlin Wu, Ferit Ozdaban, Selvanathan Sadhasivam, Xiaoyang Lu and Minxuan Zhou of Illinois Tech, with Yunhui Guo of the University of Texas at Dallas, moved the memory-bound operations of hyperbolic machine learning models into processing-in-memory units, leaving compute-dense work on the GPU. On HypFormer datasets the design ran 3 to 7 times faster than an A100 GPU and cut total energy by an average of 30% for a single inference task.

entry.title: The case for context engineering in scientific AI
entry.summary: In February 2026 talks at Illinois Tech and ESIP, Anthony Kougkas argued that context quality, not model size, decides whether AI agents work in science.
entry.content:
On February 17, 2026, Anthony Kougkas spoke at the monthly meeting of Earth Science Information Partners (ESIP) on context engineering for environmental data systems. His argument, first made at an Illinois Tech seminar six days earlier, was that AI agents in science fail or succeed on the quality of the context they receive, not on the size of the model.

Infrastructure built for a different user​

Environmental data systems were designed for human-driven batch workflows. AI agents need something else: real-time, semantic access to archives stored as HDF5, NetCDF and Zarr, which are growing to petabyte scale. Kougkas defined context engineering as "the discipline of building dynamic systems that deliver the right data, metadata, and tools to AI agents at the right time."

The point builds on earlier GRC work on the gap between scientific data and AI. DLIO, a benchmark for the I/O behavior of scientific deep learning applications, won the CCGrid 2021 best paper award. Stimulus (CCGrid 2022) showed that scientific formats such as HDF5 and NetCDF remain incompatible with AI frameworks unless the data is converted by hand. The ESIP talk took the next step and examined the gap between what current storage systems provide and what autonomous agents need.

How context goes wrong​

The ESIP talk identified four context failure modes that appear at archive scale: poisoning, rot, clash and overflow. The seminar described the first in detail. In context poisoning, bad data enters an agent workflow and cascades through it until it corrupts the scientific result.

Both talks answered with the same four core strategies for managing context: write, select, compress and isolate. They follow from the definition above: context is delivered by a dynamic system, not written once into a prompt.

From a chatbot to a multi-agent system​

At the February 11 computer science doctoral seminar at Illinois Tech, titled "From Storage Optimization to Context Orchestration: Why Your AI Infrastructure is Already Obsolete", Kougkas gave a live demonstration that contrasted a single chatbot with a multi-agent system. The demonstration used orchestrator patterns, meta-prompting and human-in-the-loop design to show the infrastructure that separates a demo from autonomous science that holds up in production. The talk also asked whether the future belongs to general-purpose agents or to domain-specific scientific systems, and mapped open problems in context quality metrics, provenance tracking and evaluation frameworks. In both talks, the stated aim was to amplify scientific intuition, not replace scientists, by automating tedious data orchestration so researchers can focus on discovery.

Where IOWarp fits​

Both talks presented IOWarp, GRC's NSF-funded platform for scientific data, as the systems answer. IOWarp places data across memory and storage tiers and exposes it to agents. Its CLIO Kit component provides Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers for scientific data formats, so an agent can query an HDF5 or NetCDF file through a standard interface instead of a custom conversion script. ESIP published the recording of the session.

Update (May 2026): Kougkas carried the same argument into genomics as a featured keynote speaker at the 7th IFSH High-Throughput Sequencing Symposium, held May 19 and 20, 2026, in Burr Ridge, Illinois, and organized by Illinois Tech's Institute for Food Safety and Health. His talk on May 20, "IOWarp: Intelligent Data Management to Accelerate Food Safety Genomic Research", applied IOWarp to the data handling in genomic analysis.

entry.title: Jaime Cernuda and Luke Logan join the research faculty
entry.summary: Two GRC-trained systems researchers become assistant research professors at Illinois Tech, and Bogdan Nicolae of Argonne joins the center the same month.
entry.content:
Jaime Cernuda and Luke Logan became assistant research professors at Illinois Institute of Technology in January 2026. Both trained as PhD students in the Gnosis Research Center and stay with it, carrying their work on storage and data movement into IOWarp, the lab's NSF-funded platform for scientific data and AI agents.

Luke Logan: storage that programs can shape​

Logan first joined Illinois Tech as an undergraduate researcher in 2017 and began his PhD in 2020. His degree was conferred in December 2025. His research asks how to make distributed storage and operating systems more programmable, portable and fast, and each of his main systems answers part of that question:

  • LabStor (SC22) is a modular platform for building customized, high-performance I/O stacks in user space.
  • MegaMmap (SC24) is a software distributed shared memory that tiers DRAM with NVMe, SSD and HDD, so applications can work on datasets larger than memory without writing out-of-core code. Logan presented it in Atlanta; the SC24 article covers the design and results.
  • pMEMCPY (REX-IO 2021) is a small, portable I/O library for storing data in persistent memory.

He also co-authored an evaluation of the DAOS object store for simulation and deep learning workloads, first at the CHEOPS 2023 workshop and then in ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review in 2024.

Jaime Cernuda: data as streams​

Cernuda joined the lab in August 2020 and defended his dissertation in late 2025. His work treats scientific data as something in motion, moving through tiers of storage and stages of analysis:

  • HFlow (CLUSTER 2021) is a dynamic, elastic, multi-layered data forwarder.
  • Hades (CCGrid 2024) is a context-aware I/O layer that computes selected quantities while simulation data is in transit, so later analysis queries do not have to traverse large files again.
  • HStream (ICPP 2024) is a hierarchical data streaming engine for high-throughput scientific applications.
  • Jarvis (PDSW 2024) is an extensible Python framework that deploys, manages and monitors software on heterogeneous HPC clusters, with pipelines that stay portable across machines.

What they work on now​

Both have been on the IOWarp team since the project started in August 2024. IOWarp is funded by an NSF framework grant shared with the University of Utah. It organizes scientific data, metadata, telemetry and computational state so that workflows and AI agents can find and use them. MegaMmap and Jarvis are both part of the IOWarp publication record. Logan and Cernuda are also the two main developers of Jarvis-CD (opens in a new tab), the open-source tool behind the Jarvis paper, and they now carry that work forward as researchers rather than students.

A third faculty arrival​

Bogdan Nicolae also joined GRC in January 2026. He is a computer scientist at Argonne National Laboratory and holds a Research Professor appointment at Illinois Tech. His research covers fault tolerance, checkpointing and data management for HPC and AI, and he received a DOE Early Career Research Program award (opens in a new tab) in 2020. He leads the Illinois Tech part of MPI4AI, an NSF project that extends Open MPI for large-scale AI training and inference, and has worked with GRC since 2023 as an Argonne partner on the DOE-funded DTIO project.

entry.title: The modern HPC+AI researcher: from specialist to orchestrator
entry.summary: Anthony Kougkas argues that the scarcest research skill is now orchestrating compute, data, AI agents and expert judgment, not deep knowledge of one task.
entry.content:
The capability of artificial intelligence to undertake complex tasks is growing at a pace that defies easy extrapolation. For those of us who have spent careers building the infrastructure that makes large-scale computation possible, this moment feels less like a disruption and more like a culmination, the point at which the systems we build must finally become as intelligent as the science they serve. The question facing every PhD student, every research engineer, and every principal investigator in High-Performance Computing is not whether AI will reshape the research process, but whether they will be the ones directing that transformation.

This is the argument I want to make: the scarcest resource in modern research is no longer deep knowledge of a specific task. It is the ability to orchestrate compute, capital, data, and expert judgment to produce new outcomes. The age of the specialist executor is giving way to the age of the agent orchestrator, and the researchers who internalize this shift earliest will define the next decade of scientific discovery.

Expertise reimagined: from knowing to designing research loops​

The traditional premium on comprehensive domain expertise, knowing every detail of a specific algorithm, every parameter of a simulation framework, every corner case of a storage protocol, is not disappearing. It is being repositioned. Deep knowledge remains the foundation, but its power is now amplified most when embedded into AI-driven workflows rather than held exclusively in a single researcher's head.

Consider the trajectory. A decade ago, the highest-impact researcher in an HPC lab was the person who could write the fastest MPI code, tune the most parameters, and run the most complex simulations end-to-end. That skill set still matters. But the researcher who will have the greatest impact over the next decade is the one who can design the research loop, the one who architects systems in which AI agents explore vast parameter spaces, analyze intermediate results, flag ambiguities for human review, and iterate toward solutions with minimal manual intervention.

This is not a hypothetical future. It is the design philosophy behind projects like IOWarp and DaYu, where our work has evolved from building tools that researchers operate to building platforms that researchers direct. The distinction is subtle but consequential: the former requires the researcher to be present at every step; the latter requires the researcher to be present at the right steps, the ones where human judgment, domain intuition, and creative hypothesis generation are genuinely irreplaceable.

The practical implication for PhD students is direct: invest in learning how to decompose research problems into components that can be delegated to intelligent systems, and components that require your irreplaceable expertise. The goal is not to automate yourself out of relevance, but to amplify your relevance by orders of magnitude.

Resource orchestration as a core competency​

In a world where you can spin up thousands of AI agents or launch massively parallel simulations on demand, the bottleneck shifts from individual task completion to the strategic allocation of finite resources. Your HPC cluster has a fixed number of nodes. Your computational budget has a ceiling. Access to unique experimental datasets is constrained. And your own time, the hours you spend reviewing results, refining hypotheses, and making judgment calls, is the scarcest resource of all.

The modern researcher must become fluent in a new kind of resource management:

  • Compute allocation: When do you burn GPU-hours on broad exploration versus targeted refinement? When is it worth running that 10,000-node simulation, and when is a well-designed surrogate model sufficient?
  • Energy-aware scheduling: As energy costs become a first-class concern in HPC operations, the ability to schedule intensive workloads during off-peak windows or in regions with cheaper power is not just an operations problem, it is a research design problem.
  • Human-in-the-loop budgeting: Perhaps the most underappreciated resource question is when to invest your own attention. An effective orchestrator knows which intermediate results to inspect personally and which to delegate to automated validation pipelines.

This is fundamentally an optimization problem, and it is one that HPC researchers are uniquely well-equipped to solve, if they recognize it as part of their job description. Resource orchestration is not administrative overhead. It is a core research competency, and it will increasingly separate high-impact labs from the rest.

At GRC, this thinking is reflected in how we approach projects like WisIO, which automates I/O bottleneck detection across entire workflow pipelines, and DTIO, which expresses I/O as composable, replayable tasks. Both embody the principle that the infrastructure itself should be intelligent enough to optimize resource utilization, freeing the researcher to focus on the science.

Agent literacy: the new foundational skill​

Just as proficiency with version control, scripting, and statistical software became baseline expectations for researchers over the past two decades, literacy in designing, managing, and auditing AI agent workflows will become a foundational skill within the next five years. This goes well beyond prompt engineering. It is closer to product management for AI-driven research.

What does agent literacy look like in practice?

  1. Decomposition: Breaking a complex research question into sub-tasks that AI can meaningfully assist with, and sub-tasks that require human expertise.
  2. Objective specification: Defining clear, measurable objectives for AI agents, not just "analyze this dataset" but "identify statistically significant deviations from the baseline model at the 95% confidence level, and rank them by potential impact on the hypothesis."
  3. Output auditing: Developing robust habits for evaluating AI-generated results. This means understanding failure modes, recognizing hallucination patterns, and building verification pipelines that catch errors before they propagate.
  4. Iterative refinement: Treating AI workflows the way good engineers treat any system, with continuous testing, A/B experimentation, and iterative improvement. The first version of an AI-assisted research pipeline will not be the best version. The discipline of systematic refinement is what compounds impact over time.

This is why emerging work like the agentic memory direction of ChronoLog, which coordinates memory for multi-agent systems, and CLIO GenomIO, which develops context-aware AI agents for genomic data orchestration, represents a pedagogical contribution as well as a technical one. They are defining the design patterns that the next generation of researchers will need to internalize.

The orchestrator's mandate​

The argument I am making is not that deep technical skill is becoming less important. It is that deep technical skill, by itself, is no longer sufficient for maximum impact. The researchers who will lead the next era of scientific discovery will be the ones who combine three capabilities:

  1. Domain expertise deep enough to know which questions matter and which results to trust.
  2. Systems thinking broad enough to design intelligent pipelines that use heterogeneous resources, from HPC clusters to AI agents to human collaborators.
  3. Orchestration discipline rigorous enough to manage the complexity that emerges when all of these capabilities are composed into a single research operation.

The capability of AI to undertake complex tasks is growing exponentially. The cost of compute continues to fall. The volume of data continues to rise. In this environment, the premium shifts decisively toward judgment, the ability to determine what to compute, when, with what resources, and to what end.

As you progress in your PhD, I encourage you to embrace this shift deliberately. Do not simply learn to use AI tools. Learn to direct them. Learn to build systems that make your research more efficient, more rigorous, and more ambitious than any individual, no matter how talented, could achieve alone.

This is the Age of the Agent Orchestrator. The infrastructure is being built. The question is whether you are ready to lead it.

entry.title: HPCC 2025 keynote: from parallel computing to concurrent data access
entry.summary: At IEEE HPCC 2025 in Exeter, Xian-He Sun argued that parallel computing and multicore designs worsen the memory wall and proposed dataflow under von Neumann.
entry.content:
Xian-He Sun gave a keynote at the 27th IEEE International Conference on High Performance Computing and Communications (HPCC 2025) in Exeter, UK, which ran from August 13 to 15, 2025. In "From Parallel Computing to Concurrent Data Access: The Dataflow under von Neumann Machine Approach", he argued that decades of work on faster computation have made the data access problem worse.

Speedup is not the problem anymore​

Deep learning succeeds because it can process vast amounts of data, but computing systems are struggling to keep up, and that has brought back the memory-wall problem. Sun's argument at HPCC was pointed. The tools the field relies on, parallel computing, multicore processors and dataflow architectures, were all designed to speed up computation. None was designed for the memory wall, and each puts more pressure on memory systems that are already overloaded. Data access has become the main performance limit of computing, and he called for rethinking computing from a data-centric point of view.

Concurrent data access​

The approach he proposed is dataflow under the von Neumann machine. It rests on two GRC models. The C-AMAT model measures the benefit of serving many data accesses at once and shows how locality and concurrency relate. The Layered Performance Matching (LPM) framework uses that measure to tune each layer of the memory hierarchy. Together they shift the target from parallel computation to concurrent data access, which is the move named in the talk's title.

Sun then discussed GRC's work in I/O systems, centered on the Hermes multi-tiered I/O buffering system, which uses LPM to decide how data moves between storage tiers.

Shared infrastructure​

The talk closed with ideas for computer system designs for AI and big data, and with the role of shared research infrastructure. Sun pointed to StoreHub, a proposed community facility for storage research that GRC is planning with The Ohio State University under an NSF grant, as one way to speed progress.

entry.title: PERMAVOST 2025 keynote: dataflow under the von Neumann machine
entry.summary: At PERMAVOST 2025, held with ACM HPDC 2025, Xian-He Sun presented dataflowV as a new paradigm for computing systems and posed open questions in memory modeling.
entry.content:
Xian-He Sun gave the keynote at the 5th Workshop on Performance Engineering, Modeling, Analysis, and Visualization Strategy (PERMAVOST 2025), held with ACM HPDC 2025 at the University of Notre Dame on July 20, 2025. His talk, "Dataflow under the von Neumann Machine: A New Paradigm for Computing Systems", spoke directly to the workshop's focus on performance modeling.

A paradigm for data-centric computing​

Sun started from the shift that big data and AI have caused: computing has become data-centric, so data management is now the first priority of a computing system. Traditional I/O and storage paradigms, he argued, no longer meet that demand, and a new paradigm is needed that joins high-performance computing with the velocity, volume and variety of data that different AI workloads need. He called that paradigm dataflow under the von Neumann machine, or DataflowV.

The models behind DataflowV​

The talk presented DataflowV in three steps. The Concurrent-AMAT (C-AMAT) model quantifies the benefit of concurrent data access and shows how data locality relates to concurrency; it gives a way to measure and close the performance gap at each layer of the memory hierarchy. The Layered Performance Matching (LPM) framework then optimizes a memory system layer by layer. On that base Sun defined DataflowV formally and showed results from applying it, including the Hermes multi-tiered I/O buffering system.

Open questions for performance modeling​

For a workshop on performance engineering, the last part of the talk mattered most. Sun said C-AMAT and LPM are powerful but leave many basic questions open. Have we used modern hardware advances to their full potential? Should advanced memory systems be built around concurrent-aware locality, a model of locality that also accounts for concurrency? He presented these as research problems for the modeling community rather than settled answers.

The workshop has published Sun's slides.

entry.title: SSDBM 2025 keynote: the data-centric imperative
entry.summary: At SSDBM 2025 in Columbus, Ohio, Xian-He Sun traced GRC's path from the Hermes buffering system to StoreHub, a proposed community storage research facility.
entry.content:
Xian-He Sun gave the third keynote of the 37th International Conference on Scalable Scientific Data Management (SSDBM 2025) in Columbus, Ohio, on June 24, 2025. In "The Data-Centric Imperative: from Hermes to StoreHub", he argued that storage systems must be redesigned for data-centric computing and that the community needs shared infrastructure to test those designs.

Why storage has to change​

Big data, AI and data-intensive science have made computing data-centric, and Sun argued that traditional I/O architectures and storage paradigms no longer meet that demand. Next-generation storage has to connect high-performance computing with the velocity, volume and variety of data that AI workloads bring. The keynote set out the open problems and GRC's current approaches to them.

From models to Hermes​

The technical core followed the line of Sun's 2025 talks. The C-AMAT model quantifies the benefit of concurrent data access and the relation between locality and concurrency. The Layered Performance Matching (LPM) framework uses it to tune each layer of the memory hierarchy. Together they lead to dataflow under the von Neumann machine, an approach that organizes computation around the cost of moving data. The Hermes multi-tiered I/O buffering system puts LPM into practice by deciding how data moves between storage tiers, and Sun presented it as GRC's main success in this line of work.

StoreHub​

The second half looked ahead to computer system designs for AI and big data that ease the memory wall, and to the infrastructure needed to build them. Sun described StoreHub, a proposed community facility where researchers could co-design, test and validate new storage hardware and software together. Sun leads StoreHub, with Anthony Kougkas as co-PI, under a collaborative NSF Community Infrastructure for Research in Computer and Information Science and Engineering (CIRC) planning grant with The Ohio State University. The planning project was assessing whether the community needs such a facility and what it should provide. The day before the keynote, on June 23, the first StoreHub Community Workshop took place at Ohio State alongside SSDBM 2025, with nineteen student posters.

GRC at SSDBM 2025​

Anthony Kougkas, GRC's Executive Director, served as General Vice Chair of SSDBM 2025. The conference also published Keith Bateman's paper on DTIO, a data stack for AI-driven workflows that GRC developed with Argonne National Laboratory.

entry.title: HPC Asia 2025 invited talk: dataflow under the von Neumann machine
entry.summary: At HPC Asia 2025 in Hsinchu, Xian-He Sun presented C-AMAT, LPM and dataflow under the von Neumann machine as a data-centric answer to the memory wall.
entry.content:
Xian-He Sun gave the third invited talk at HPC Asia 2025 in Hsinchu, Taiwan, on February 20, 2025. The program lists it as "Dataflow under the Von Neumann machine: A Destructive New under Existing Systems". Sun argued that the memory wall, not raw compute, now limits AI systems, and presented a data-centric approach to it.

The memory wall returns​

The success of deep learning depends on processing vast amounts of data, and computing systems are struggling to supply it. Sun argued that this demand has brought researchers back to the memory-wall problem: processors can compute far faster than memory and storage can deliver data to them. His answer is a concept he calls dataflow under the von Neumann machine, which keeps the conventional architecture but organizes computation around the cost of moving data.

Two models: C-AMAT and LPM​

The talk built the concept on two pieces of GRC research.

  • C-AMAT (Concurrent Average Memory Access Time) extends the classic average memory access time model to modern memory systems that serve many accesses at once. It counts how many hits and misses are in flight together and separates the misses that actually stall the processor from those hidden behind other work. This quantifies the benefit of concurrent data access and shows how data locality and concurrency relate.
  • LPM (Layered Performance Matching) applies C-AMAT layer by layer. It tunes each level of the memory hierarchy so that the rate at which it can supply data matches the rate at which the level above requests it, so no layer becomes the one that stalls the rest.

With these two tools in place, Sun formally introduced dataflow under the von Neumann machine.

From software to hardware​

Sun then turned to GRC's work on I/O systems, in particular the Hermes multi-tiered I/O buffering system. Hermes uses the LPM framework to decide how data moves between memory, flash and disk tiers, and Sun described it as a clear success. That raised the question at the center of the talk: Hermes is a software solution for I/O systems, so what is the practical hardware solution for memory systems? He closed with open problems and ideas for computer system designs for AI and big data that would ease the memory wall.

The venue​

HPC Asia 2025 was hosted by Taiwan's National Center for High-performance Computing (NCHC) under the theme "Chip-based Exploration and Innovation for HPC". Sun's talk ran from 13:30 to 14:20 and was chaired by Taisuke Boku.

entry.title: NPC 2024 keynote: Hermes, Coeus and ChronoLog
entry.summary: At NPC 2024 in Haikou, Xian-He Sun opened the keynotes with a survey of three GRC data systems, Hermes, Coeus and ChronoLog, aimed at the data bottleneck of AI.
entry.content:
Xian-He Sun gave the first keynote of the IFIP International Conference on Network and Parallel Computing (NPC 2024) in Haikou, China, on December 7, 2024. Titled "Hermes, Coeus, and ChronoLog: Some big data I/O systems for network, parallel and distributed computing", the talk walked through three GRC systems that each attack a different part of the data access bottleneck.

The data bottleneck in AI​

Sun started from deep learning. Its success depends on processing vast amounts of data, and computing systems are struggling to supply data fast enough, which turns I/O into the bottleneck. He argued that data access has become the main performance limit for network, parallel and distributed computing (NPC) when it serves AI, and that AI can in turn help relieve that limit. The talk looked at both directions, NPC for AI and AI for NPC, from the point of view of the I/O system.

Three systems​

Hermes is a multi-tiered I/O buffering system. It optimizes how data moves through a deep memory and storage hierarchy, from memory through local flash and burst buffers to the parallel file system. The abstract describes it as serving both directions, NPC for AI and AI for NPC.

Coeus enriches the metadata that scientific data systems keep, and uses active storage, storage that can run computation, to calculate derived quantities and answer complex queries over scientific data. The goal is to let scientists ask questions of their data without first moving all of it to compute nodes. Coeus is a collaborative project funded by the DOE Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research and led by Sandia National Laboratories, with GRC as a partner.

ChronoLog is a distributed, tiered log store for log data in cloud computing environments. It orders events by time across many nodes, so that logs from large distributed systems can be written and read at scale. ChronoLog is funded by an NSF CSSI framework grant, and its first public beta, version 1.0.0, was released in June 2024.

Sun closed with the open questions these systems raise and with ideas for computer system designs built for AI and big data. The talk extended the keynote he gave at IEEE/ACM CCGrid 2024 in May, which also covered Hermes, ChronoLog and Coeus.
